title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 4
paragraphs: _How the Four Knights Served the Lady Guinevere._

When King Arthur returned to Cameliard (this was in the afternoon of the second day), he found the gardener waiting for him, very angry. The gardener had brought a long birch rod to punish his boy with when the boy came back to the garden. When he saw King Arthur, he said, “You rascal! Why did you leave your work and go wandering off?” King Arthur laughed and said, “Do not touch me.” This made the gardener so furious that he grabbed the King by the collar of his jacket, meaning to beat him. “Are you laughing at me, you rascal, and making fun of me? Now I will give you a good beating for what you have done.”

When King Arthur felt that man’s hand on him and heard the angry words of the gardener, his royal spirit swelled up within him, and he cried out, “Ha, wretch! Would you dare to lay your hands on my sacred person?” With that, he seized the gardener by the wrists, took the rod away from him, and struck him across the shoulders with it. The poor man felt himself held in the powerful grip of the angry King, and he felt the rod on his shoulders. He let out a great cry, although the blow did not hurt him at all. “Now get out of here!” said King Arthur. “Do not trouble me again, or I will treat you in a way you will not like at all.” With that, he let the poor man go. The gardener was so dazed with terror that the earth and the sky seemed to spin around him. King Arthur’s eyes had flashed at him like lightning, and those two hands had held his wrists with wonderful strength. So when the King let him go, he hurried away as fast as he could, trembling and sweating with fear.

He went straight to the Lady Guinevere and complained to her about how he had been treated. “Lady,” he said, weeping at the memory of his fright, “my boy goes away for a day or more, and I do not know where. When I tried to whip him for leaving his work, he took the rod right out of my hands and beat me with it. So now I beg you, deal with him as he deserves, and have several strong men chase him away from this place with rods.”

The Lady Guinevere laughed. “Leave him be,” she said, “and do not bother him anymore. He seems to me a very cheeky fellow. As for you, pay no attention to his coming or going, and perhaps I will deal with him in a way that suits him.”

The gardener went away, greatly wondering why the Lady Guinevere was so gentle with that insolent rascal. The Lady Guinevere went away too, in very good spirits. She had begun to think that there was surely a good reason for what had happened. When the White Champion, who did such wonderful deeds, came to the castle, the gardener’s boy went away. When the same Champion left, the gardener’s boy came back. So she suspected many things, and she felt wonderfully merry and cheerful.

That afternoon the Lady Guinevere happened to be walking in the garden with her damsels. With her walked the four noble knights whom her White Champion had sent there: Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias. The gardener’s lad was digging in the gardens, and as they passed him, the Lady Guinevere laughed aloud and cried out, “Look! Look! My lords and ladies! There is a very cheeky fellow for a gardener’s lad. He keeps his cap on all the time, even when he stands in front of lords and ladies.”

Then Sir Gawaine spoke up. “Is that so? Then I will go to that rascal right now and take his hat off for him. I will do it so roughly that I do not believe he will ever offend us again by wearing it in our presence.”

The Lady Guinevere laughed a great deal at this. “Leave him be,” she said, “leave him be! Sir Gawaine, it would not suit someone as gentle as you to have anything to do with that cheeky fellow. Besides, he has assured us all that he has an ugly sore on his head, so let him wear his cap, and God be merciful to him.”
So the Lady Guinevere, although she suspected a very great deal, was pleased to make fun of the very person she suspected.

That day Duke Mordaunt of North Umber had fully recovered from the painful injuries he had suffered when the White Champion overthrew him. So when the next morning came, he appeared before the castle again as he had done before, dressed in full armor. This time two heralds rode in front of him. When the duke and the two heralds reached the part of the meadows right in front of the castle of Cameliard, the heralds blew their trumpets very loudly. At the sound of the trumpets, many people came and gathered on the walls. King Leodegrance came too, and he took his place on a smaller tower that looked down on the plain where the Duke of North Umber and the two heralds stood. Then the Duke of North Umber looked up and saw King Leodegrance standing above him on top of that tower, and he cried out in a loud voice, “Hello there, King Leodegrance! Do not think that you are rid of me just because I fell from my horse by the bad luck of a fight. Nevertheless, I now make you this fair offer. Tomorrow I will appear before this castle with six fellow knights. If you have any seven knights who can stand against me and my companions in a fight, whether with spears or swords, on horseback or on foot, then I will give up every claim I have to the hand of the Lady Guinevere. But if you cannot find such champions to fight successfully against me and my fellow knights, then I will not only claim Lady Guinevere, but I will also seize and keep for myself three castles of yours that stand on the borders of North Umber. I will also seize and keep all the lands and church fields that belong to those same castles. Moreover, this challenge of mine will hold only until sunset tomorrow, and after that time it will be null and void. So, King Leodegrance, you had better see to it right away that you find champions who can defend you against these demands.”

Then the two heralds blew their trumpets once more, and Duke Mordaunt of North Umber turned his horse around and rode away. King Leodegrance went away too, very sorrowful and downhearted. He said to himself, “Is it at all likely that another champion will come to me like that wonderful White Champion who came two days ago, I do not know from where, to defend me against my enemies? And as for that White Champion, if I do not know where he came from, I also do not know where he has gone. How then can I know where to look for him to beg for his help again in this time of my great need?” So he went on his way, very sorrowful, and he did not know what to do to defend himself. Troubled to the depths of his spirit, he went straight to his own room and shut himself in. He would not see anyone or speak to anyone, but gave himself up completely to sorrow and despair.

In this great need, the Lady Guinevere thought of the four knights who had promised to serve her for seven days. She went to them where they were and spoke to them like this: “My lords, you were sent here, pledged to serve me for seven days. Now I order you to take up this challenge of Duke Mordaunt at my request. I very much want you to go out tomorrow and meet this Duke of North Umber and his fellow knights in battle. You are terribly powerful knights, and I believe you can easily defend us against our enemies.”

But Sir Gawaine said, “No, Lady, no! We are pledged to your service, but we are not pledged to the service of King Leodegrance, your father. We have no quarrel of any kind with this Duke of North Umber or with his six fellow knights. We are knights of King Arthur’s Court, and we may not take up a foreign quarrel in the service of another king unless he commands it.”

Then the Lady Guinevere became extremely angry, and she said hotly, “Either you are a wonderfully faithful lord to your King, Sir Gawaine, or else you are afraid to meet this Duke of North Umber and his fellow knights.”

At these words of the Lady Guinevere, Sir Gawaine also grew very angry, and he answered, “If you were a knight and not a lady, Dame Guinevere, you would think three or four times before you found the courage to say those words to me.” With that he rose and left the place, his face red with anger. The Lady Guinevere also left and went to her chamber, where she wept a great deal, both from sorrow and from anger.

All this while King Arthur had been well aware of everything that happened. So after a while he got up, went out, and found the gardener. He took the gardener firmly by the collar of his coat and held him where he stood. He said to him, “Fellow! I have an order to give you, and you will carry it out exactly, or else a great deal of pain may come to you.” As he spoke, he thrust his hand into the front of his jacket and brought out the necklace of pearls that the Lady Guinevere had given him from around her own neck. And he said to the gardener, “You will take this necklace to the Lady Guinevere and say this to her: she is to send me at once bread and meat and wine and sweets from her own table. Tell her that I want her to call those four knights, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias, and that she is to order them to come and serve me with those things for my refreshment. Tell her also that she is to command those knights to go on serving me as I direct, and that from now on they are to be my servants and not hers. These are the orders I give you: you are to say these things to the Lady Guinevere.”

When the gardener heard those words, he was so astonished that he did not know what to think, for he believed the gardener’s lad had gone completely mad. He raised his voice and cried aloud, “What is this! What are you saying? Truly, if I do what you tell me, it will cost me my life or else it will cost you yours. Who would dare to say such words to the Lady Guinevere?”

But King Arthur said, “Nevertheless, you will do as I command you, fellow. If you fail in even one point, I assure you it will go very badly for you. I have the power to make you suffer as you have never suffered before.”

At this the gardener said, “I will go.” He said to himself, “If I do as this fellow tells me, the Lady Guinevere will have him severely punished, and so I will get my revenge for what he did to me yesterday. Besides, it annoys me very much to have a lad working in the garden who behaves as this fellow does. So,” he said, “I will go.” He took the necklace of pearls that King Arthur gave him and went out, and after a while he found the Lady Guinevere. When he had found her, he spoke to her like this:

“Lady, my garden boy has surely gone completely mad. He threatened to do me great harm if I did not carry out his errand, and he has sent me to give you a very grievous insult. He sent me with this string of large beads to give to you. He tells me to say that you are to send him bread and meat and sweets and wine, such as you use at your own table. He tells me to say that these things are to be served to him by the four noble knights who came here the day before yesterday. He says that you are to command those same knights to obey him in whatever he orders, for from now on they are to be his servants and not yours. And truly, Lady, he would listen to nothing I said against it, but threatened me with dire injury if I did not come here and deliver this message to you.”

When the Lady Guinevere heard what the gardener said, and when she saw the necklace that she had given to the White Champion, she knew that the White Champion and the gardener’s boy were one and the same. She was filled with such great joy that she did not know whether to laugh or to weep. She got up and took the necklace of pearls, and she told the gardener to come with her. Then she went until she found the four knights, and when she had found them, she spoke to them like this:

“My lords, a little while ago I commanded you to take up my quarrel with Duke Mordaunt of North Umber for my sake, and you would not do it. And you, my lord Gawaine, spoke such angry words as a servant should not speak to his mistress, still less a knight to the daughter of a king. So I have decided that you will do a certain thing as a penance. If you refuse, I will know very well that you do not mean to keep the promise you gave to my knight when he overthrew all four of you in fair combat. This is my command: you will take food prepared for my table, meats and white bread and sweets and wine, and you will take that food to my gardener’s boy, whose cap you so bravely threatened to take away this very morning, Sir Gawaine. All four of you are to serve the food to him as though he were a royal knight. And when you have served him, you are to obey him in whatever he orders. I put this on you as a penalty because you did not take up my quarrel as true knights should. From now on you are to be servants to that gardener’s boy and not to me. So go now to the buttery of the castle, and tell the steward to give you meats such as are served at my own table. You are to serve the food on silver plates, and the wine in silver cups and goblets. And you are to wait on that gardener’s boy as though he were a great lord of enormous fame and renown.”

So spoke the Lady Guinevere, and when she had finished speaking, she turned and left the four knights. She took the gardener with her, and he was so astonished at what he had heard that he did not know whether he had gone mad or whether the Lady Guinevere had gone mad. The Lady Guinevere told the gardener to go to the gardener’s boy and tell him that everything would be done as he commanded. And the gardener did as he was told.

Now let us turn to the four knights whom the Lady Guinevere had left behind. They were bewildered and ashamed at the strange commands she had given them. When they recovered from their amazement, they burned with such great anger that, for a while, they could not tell whether what they saw was daylight or complete darkness. None of them could look another in the face, so overcome were they with shame at the insult they had received. Then Sir Gawaine spoke up, and his voice shook so much with anger that he could hardly get the words out. “Messires,” he said, “do you not see how this lady has deliberately insulted us? She did it because we refused to do what she told us this morning, and because we would not take up her quarrel against the Duke of North Umber. Well, we will serve this gardener’s boy just as she has ordered. We will bring him food and drink as she commanded, and we will wait on him as she told us to. But mark this: we are no longer her servants. We are his servants, and so we may serve him in whatever way we choose. So when we have carried out her orders, and served him food and drink, and obeyed every command he gives us, then I make this vow. I will kill that gardener’s boy with my own hand. When he is dead, I will put his head into a bag, and I will send the bag to the Lady Guinevere by the humblest carrier I can find. In that way this proud lady will receive an insult as great as the one she has given us.” And they all agreed that everything should happen exactly as Sir Gawaine had said.

So the four lords went to the steward of the castle, and they asked for the best of the food that was to be served to the Lady Guinevere: meats and bread and sweet cakes and wine. Then they took silver plates and platters and set the food upon them. They took silver cups and goblets and poured the wine into them, and they went out carrying these things. Behind the castle, near the stables, they found the gardener’s boy, and they told him to sit down and eat and drink. They waited on him as if he were some great lord. Not one of the four knights knew who he really was. They did not know that he was the great King whom, in truth, they served. He wore his cap of disguise upon his head, and so they thought he was only a poor peasant.

Now Sir Ewaine saw that the boy still kept his cap on before them, and he spoke to him in great anger, saying, “Ha, villain! Would you keep your cap on even in the presence of great princes and lords such as we are?”
Sir Gawaine said, “Leave it, it does not matter.” Then he spoke very bitterly to the gardener’s boy. “Eat well, fellow! For you will hardly eat another meal on this earth.”

The gardener’s boy answered, “Sir Knight, perhaps that will be decided by a will other than yours. I may eat many more meals than this one. And perhaps you will wait on me at them, as you are waiting on me now.” The four lords were astonished beyond measure that he could speak to them so calmly and without any sign of fear.

When he had finished eating, the gardener’s boy said to the knights, “Look, Messires, I have had enough and I am done. Now I have other commands for you to carry out. My next command is that you get ready at once to ride out with me, and for that you must put on full armor. And you, Sir Gawaine, will go to the head stable-keeper of this castle and tell him to prepare the Lady Guinevere’s palfrey, so that I may ride out on it right away. When you are all dressed in your armor, and everything is ready as I have commanded, bring that palfrey to the back gate of the castle. I will meet you there, and we will ride out together.”
Sir Gawaine said, “It shall be done exactly as you command. But when we ride out from this castle, it will be a sorry journey for you.”
The gardener’s boy said, “I do not think so, Sir Gawaine.”

Then the four went away and did as the gardener’s boy had commanded. When they were dressed in full armor and had fetched the Lady Guinevere’s palfrey, they went to the back gate, and there the gardener’s boy met them. He saw that they stayed seated on their horses and did not move when he came. So he said, “Ha, Messires! Is this how you treat the one you have been ordered to serve? Now I command you, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, to come down and hold my stirrup for me. And I command you, Sir Geraint and Sir Pellias, to come down and hold my palfrey while I mount.”

Then the four noble knights did as they were told. And Sir Gawaine said, “You may give orders as you please, and I advise you to make the most of it while you can. You have only a little while left to enjoy the great honor that has come to you. For that honor, look you, will soon crush you to death.”
The gardener’s boy said, “Not so. I believe I will not die for a good while yet.” Again the four lords were greatly astonished at how calm he was.
So they rode out from that place. The gardener’s boy would not allow them to ride in front of him or beside him. He ordered them to ride behind him, since they were still his servants.

They rode that way, as he had arranged, for a long distance. After they had gone a great way forward, they came near a gloomy and dismal forest. It lay just beyond the lands that border Cameliard. When they were close to this forest, Sir Gawaine rode a little ahead and said, “Sir Gardener’s Boy, do you see that forest over there? When we enter it, you will die at once, and by a sword that has never been touched by anyone but noble or knightly blood.”
King Arthur turned around in his saddle and said, “Ha! Sir Gawaine! Would you ride ahead like this when I have told you to ride behind me?”
As he spoke he took the cap from his head, and then they all saw that it was King Arthur who rode with them.

Then a great silence of utter astonishment fell upon them all, and each man sat as still as if he had been turned into a stone statue. King Arthur was the first to speak. He said, “Ha! What is this, Sir Knights? Have you no words of greeting to offer me? Truly, you have served me very ungraciously this day. And you have even threatened to kill me. Now that I speak to you, you say nothing at all in reply.”

Then the four knights cried out at once. They leaped down from their horses and knelt in the dust of the road. When King Arthur saw them kneeling there, he laughed with great joy. He told them to mount their horses again, for time was passing and there was much to do.

So they mounted their horses and rode away. As they traveled, the King told them everything that had happened to him. They were greatly amazed, and they praised the knightly way he had behaved in all those fine adventures. They rejoiced that they had a king to rule over them who had such a high and knightly spirit.
So they rode to the part of the forest where King Arthur had left his horse and his armor.
